sections.heading: Listen for concrete next steps, not compliments
sections.content: Polite reactions such as “super interesting,” “please update me,” or “I’d love to hear more” aren’t strong buying signals on their own. Stronger signs are questions about pricing and cost, asking when a POV can start and how long it takes, or offering to connect you with the right person on their team. In B2B, look for interest that reaches the team that will actually test and deploy the tool.

sections.heading: Check for customer pull and commitment
sections.content: Raaz said founders naturally want affirmation, so deliberately tune in to whether prospects are intently interested and pushing toward action. She didn’t want to push someone into a POV if they weren’t committed; she wanted to feel the customer’s desire for the product and get “pull” from their side. She also agreed that taking a friction-heavy action, such as filling out a long questionnaire, can show extra effort and interest.

answer.summary: Raaz said not to mistake “this is interesting” or “keep me updated” for buying intent. Look for customers who actively pull the process forward and show real commitment.

sections.heading: Look for concrete buying behavior
sections.content: The signals Raaz learned to watch for were questions such as how the product is priced and what it will cost; asking when they can start a POV (proof of value) and how long it takes; or identifying exactly whom on their team to connect with. In B2B, that connection should reach the team that will test and deploy the tool. She described the difference as genuine passion—“I want this right now”—rather than polite praise or a request to be kept updated.

sections.heading: Seek customer pull, not affirmation
sections.content: Raaz cautioned that founders naturally want affirmation, so they should tune in to evidence of intent rather than treating a positive reaction as validation. She said not to push someone into a POV if they are not committed: especially while the product is still being built, she wanted to feel the customer’s commitment and pull from the other side, not push too hard.

sections.heading: How they learned to spot the difference
sections.content: At the start, Wiz made 10–15 customer calls a day, often presenting an idea before they had a solid product. Raaz contrasted calls that ended with “sounds interesting” and “I’d love to hear more” with ones that turned into specific questions about price, a POV, or introductions to the right teammates.
